questions.prompt: Put these steps of configuring LTV's enterprise structure (lesson 4) in the order they actually have to happen.
items: Create the legal entity — a standalone object with no ledger or chart of accounts reference yet
Create the primary ledger, assigning it a legal entity, chart of accounts structure, calendar, and currency
Create the business unit, referencing an existing primary ledger
Verify in Manage Primary Ledgers and Manage Business Units that each object's reference actually shows up
questions.explain: Configuration order matters because each object references the one before it: the legal entity is created first since it doesn't yet reference anything, the primary ledger second because it needs a legal entity to assign, and the business unit last because it needs an existing primary ledger to reference. Verifying both assignments afterward catches a silently blocked setup before it blocks transaction entry in Chapter 2.

questions.prompt: LTV Manufacturing Corporation's enterprise structure design (lesson 3) assigns the US parent and the Canadian subsidiary to two separate primary ledgers instead of one. Which statement correctly explains why?
options: A primary ledger has exactly one currency; the US entity reports in USD and the Canadian entity reports in CAD, so that currency difference alone requires two ledgers.
Oracle Fusion never allows two legal entities to post to the same primary ledger, no matter what currency each one uses.
Each legal entity must use its own distinct chart of accounts structure, so one ledger can't serve both.
Each legal entity must use its own distinct accounting calendar, so one ledger can't serve both.
Two primary ledgers are required simply because the two entities operate in different countries, independent of currency.

A single primary ledger can only ever be referenced by one business unit at a time, and since LTV has two business units — one per entity — two separate primary ledgers are required for that reason alone.
questions.explain: A primary ledger has exactly one currency. LTV's two legal entities have different statutory reporting currencies — USD for the US parent, CAD for the Canadian subsidiary — and that currency difference is the single fact driving the two-ledger design. Both ledgers still share the same chart of accounts structure and calendar; only the currency and legal entity differ.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B sounds like a hard platform rule, which makes it tempting, but it's wrong on the one detail that matters: Oracle Fusion does support multiple legal entities under a single ledger when they share the same ledger currency. LTV's two entities specifically can't share a ledger because USD and CAD are different currencies, not because sharing a ledger is categorically forbidden.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about LTV Manufacturing Corporation's chart of accounts design, per lesson 5.
options: The Company segment (1000 for the US, 2000 for Canada) is the balancing segment, and must net to zero for each entity within its own ledger.
The same three cost centers — Assembly (410), Fabrication (420), and Corporate Overhead (510) — exist in both the US and Canadian entities.
The Intercompany segment uses entirely different values from the Company segment, since the two segments track unrelated information.
A cross-validation rule restricts an entity from recording an intercompany value equal to its own Company value, so an intercompany leg always names the other entity.
The Future segment (segment 5) is actively used to track department-level detail beyond cost center.
questions.explain: The Company segment is the balancing segment, with 1000 and 2000 for the two entities. All three cost centers exist in both entities. The Intercompany segment deliberately mirrors the Company segment's own values (1000, 2000), not different ones, and a cross-validation rule blocks an entity from naming itself as its own intercompany partner. The Future segment is reserved with no values enabled — it isn't used for anything yet.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in LTV's chart of accounts, the Company segment value used on every transaction belonging to LTV Manufacturing Canada ULC is ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 5's Company segment table assigns 1000 to the US parent, LTV Manufacturing Corporation, and 2000 to the Canadian subsidiary, LTV Manufacturing Canada ULC — the balancing segment value every Canadian transaction must carry.

questions.prompt: Match each person from lesson 2 to their actual role at LTV Manufacturing Corporation.
right: Corporate Controller — owns the period close and GL
questions.explain: Elena Marsh is the CFO and executive sponsor. Victor Okafor is the Corporate Controller who owns the period close and GL. Chen Liu is the AP Manager. Mateo Rios is the AR Manager. Grace Olsen is the Treasury / Cash Management Analyst — each one reappears in exactly this role throughout Chapters 2 and 3.

questions.prompt: Match each of LTV's four suppliers (lesson 6) to what it actually supplies.
questions.explain: Meridian Bearing Supply Co. supplies bearings and mechanical MRO parts and is LTV's preferred supplier for that category. Palmetto Steel & Alloy Supply supplies raw steel for Fabrication. Vantage Electrical Components Inc. supplies electrical components for control panels. Crescent Freight Logistics handles inbound and outbound freight.

questions.prompt: LTV's Canadian operating bank account — Royal Bank of Canada, Windsor, ON, account ending 4420 — is linked to which natural account and Company segment value combination?
options: 1110 (Cash — Operating) at Company 2000
1110 (Cash — Operating) at Company 1000
1210 (Accounts Receivable — Trade) at Company 2000
1110 (Cash — Operating) at Company 2000, but recorded in USD
questions.explain: Lesson 8 links each bank account to account 1110 (Cash — Operating) at the Company value matching its entity — 1000 for Regions Bank (US) and 2000 for Royal Bank of Canada. The Canadian account is denominated in CAD, consistent with lesson 3's currency-driven design, not USD.

questions.prompt: LTV configures five fixed asset categories in lesson 8, each with a different useful life. Which pairing of category and useful life is correct, and becomes the exact distinction Chapter 2 tests when a CNC lathe gets capitalized?
options: Manufacturing Equipment — Machinery, 10-year life, versus Office Equipment, 5-year life
Manufacturing Equipment — Machinery, 5-year life, versus Office Equipment, 10-year life
Computer Equipment, 10-year life, versus Building & Leasehold Improvements, 3-year life
Manufacturing Equipment — Machinery, 7-year life, versus Furniture & Fixtures, 15-year life
questions.explain: Lesson 8's category table assigns Manufacturing Equipment — Machinery a 10-year useful life and Office Equipment a 5-year useful life. The lesson flags these two specifically as the pair to remember, since assigning a capitalized asset to the wrong one of these two categories produces a real, calculable depreciation difference — exactly what lessons 14 and 15 later demonstrate.

questions.prompt: Dana Whitfield's requisition for 50 units of Industrial Pump Bearing PB-4400 charges account 1000-420-1410-0000-000. Why is this charged to account 1410 (Inventory — Raw Materials) instead of an expense account?
options: PB-4400 is a stocked item held in inventory, so receiving it increases an asset account rather than an immediate expense.
Fabrication's cost center code (420) determines that all its purchases post to inventory rather than expense.
Any purchase order over $10,000.00 is automatically charged to an asset account instead of an expense account.
Meridian Bearing Supply Co. is configured so that everything purchased from it posts to inventory, regardless of the item.
questions.explain: PB-4400 is a stocked MRO item held in inventory rather than expensed on receipt, so the requisition and the purchase order it becomes both charge account 1410 (Inventory — Raw Materials), an asset account — a property of the item itself, not of the cost center, the dollar amount, or the supplier.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: at the December 31 close, journal JE-GRNI-1231 debits Inventory clearing and credits Accrued Liabilities (2150) for $________, reclassifying PO-55210's received-but-not-invoiced bearings into a formal accrual.
questions.explain: PO-55210's 50 units of PB-4400 at $368.00 each total $18,400.00 — received December 28 but not yet invoiced at December 31 close, which is exactly the amount the GRNI journal reclassifies into Accrued Liabilities.

questions.prompt: Chen Liu enters Meridian's invoice INV-MER-88341 in January, and it matches PO-55210 and the December receipt perfectly, with no price or quantity variance, and validates cleanly. Despite this, a real problem exists. What is it, and where does it actually live?
options: JE-GRNI-1231, December's accrual journal, was never flagged to auto-reverse, so the accrual is still sitting on the books when the correct January invoice posts, double-counting the liability.
The three-way match itself is flawed, because PO-55210's quantity doesn't actually match the December receipt quantity.
INV-MER-88341 was entered under the wrong supplier site, so it never actually matches PO-55210 at all.
Meridian's invoice is dated incorrectly, which causes Oracle Fusion to post it into the wrong accounting period.
questions.explain: The invoice, the PO, and the receipt are all individually correct — the problem is one level up, in December's accrual journal, which was supposed to auto-reverse on January 1 so the real invoice wouldn't double-count the liability. The auto-reverse flag was left unchecked, so the accrual is still there when the clean, correctly matched invoice posts.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the two Meridian payments Chen Liu processes in lesson 11.
options: Oracle Fusion's own records show exactly one payment event for each invoice, with no duplicates on LTV's side.
PMT-21087's $9,200.00 payment file was transmitted to Regions Bank twice because Chen Liu submitted the Payment Process Request twice by mistake.
The duplicate $9,200.00 debit happened because of a network timeout retry on the bank's own ACH processor, not because of anything inside Oracle Fusion.
Both PMT-21094 and PMT-21087 debit Accounts Payable — Trade (2110) and credit Cash — Operating (1110) in Oracle Fusion.
Meridian's bank account received two $18,400.00 credits instead of one.
questions.explain: Oracle Fusion's records are completely correct — one payment event per invoice, transmitted once. The duplicate debit happened on the bank's own ACH processor due to a network timeout retry, not because Chen Liu resubmitted anything. Both payments post with the standard AP-to-Cash entry. It's the $9,200.00 PMT-21087 payment that was duplicated at the bank, not the $18,400.00 PMT-21094 payment.

questions.prompt: A Subledger Accounting transaction has no applicable Account Rule mapping for the account it needs to credit. Which statement correctly describes what happens when Create Accounting processes it?
options: Create Accounting fails for the entire batch of transactions, not just the ones missing a rule, so nothing in that batch posts to the General Ledger.

Create Accounting marks that transaction's accounting status as Incomplete, and it isn't transferred to the General Ledger until the missing Account Rule mapping is added and Create Accounting is rerun.
Create Accounting marks that transaction's accounting status as Incomplete, but posts it anyway to a default suspense account in the General Ledger.
Create Accounting posts the transaction to the GL immediately and flags it afterward for someone to review manually.
Create Accounting rejects the transaction outright, requiring it to be voided and re-entered from scratch.

Create Accounting silently reroutes the transaction to whichever natural account number happens to be numerically closest to the one actually configured, without ever flagging it as incomplete or requiring any rule to be fixed.
questions.explain: A transaction with no applicable Account Rule gets marked accounting status Incomplete and simply doesn't transfer to the General Ledger — it stays stuck exactly where it is until the missing mapping is added and Create Accounting runs again. Other transactions that do have a valid rule are unaffected; only the ones actually missing a rule are held back.
questions.distractorExplain: Option C gets the 'Incomplete' status right, which is what makes it tempting — but it adds a wrong claim on top: an Incomplete transaction doesn't post anywhere, suspense account or otherwise. It stays unposted until the missing Account Rule mapping is added and Create Accounting is rerun, which is the one detail that makes C wrong.

questions.prompt: Harborview wires $55,100.00 for INV-HV-30144, and Mateo Rios applies the full receipt to INV-HV-29890 instead, by mistake. What effect does this actually have on Harborview's account and on LTV's total AR and cash balances?
options: INV-HV-29890 shows a $49,000.00 credit balance and INV-HV-30144 still shows open and overdue, but the total AR balance and total cash balance for Harborview are both unaffected.
Both invoices show as paid in full, and the total AR balance for Harborview drops by $55,100.00 twice.
The $55,100.00 payment is rejected because it doesn't match the amount of the invoice it's applied to.
INV-HV-30144 is marked paid even though the receipt was applied to INV-HV-29890, because Oracle Fusion automatically corrects misapplied receipts above a threshold.
questions.explain: A misapplied receipt is still a validly applied one — Oracle Fusion doesn't require a receipt's amount to match the invoice it's applied to. The cash and total AR control account are completely correct; only the open-item detail moves to the wrong invoice, which is exactly why this kind of error is invisible in a bank reconciliation or trial balance and only visible in AR aging detail.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about how FA-10452, the new CNC lathe, is actually capitalized in lesson 14.
options: The asset is capitalized to the Office Equipment category, with a 5-year useful life, instead of the correct Manufacturing Equipment — Machinery category with a 10-year life.
The asset is capitalized to cost center 410 (Assembly) instead of the correct cost center 420 (Fabrication), where the machine physically sits.
Capitalizing FA-10452 under these values causes Oracle Fusion to reject the transaction with a validation error.
Derek Shaw copied the category and cost center from an unrelated office furniture purchase approved the same week, rather than from the CNC lathe's own capital approval paperwork.
The mistake is caught immediately because Office Equipment is not a valid category for machinery placed on a Fabrication floor.
questions.explain: FA-10452 is capitalized to Office Equipment (5-year life) and cost center 410, both wrong — the correct values are Manufacturing Equipment — Machinery (10-year life) and cost center 420. Derek carried both values forward from the row above his, an unrelated office furniture purchase, rather than the lathe's own paperwork. Office Equipment and cost center 410 are both perfectly valid values, so the transaction capitalizes cleanly with no error and no immediate warning.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: FA-10452 depreciates at $2,416.67 for January as miscategorized, versus a correct $1,208.33 under Manufacturing Equipment — Machinery. That's a monthly overstatement of exactly $________.
questions.explain: $2,416.67 minus $1,208.33 leaves a difference of $1,208.34 — January's depreciation expense overstatement, which would recur every month the asset stayed miscategorized.

questions.prompt: Put these events in the Meridian bearing purchase's actual chronological order, per lessons 9-10.
items: Dana Whitfield creates a requisition for 50 units of Industrial Pump Bearing PB-4400
Marcus Ibarra converts the approved requisition into PO-55210, dated December 22
Priya Nandan records the full receipt against PO-55210 on December 28
Victor Okafor's team posts JE-GRNI-1231 at the December 31 close, without the auto-reverse flag set
Chen Liu enters Meridian's invoice INV-MER-88341 on January 14, which matches and validates cleanly
questions.explain: The requisition is created and approved first, then converted into PO-55210 on December 22. The bearings are received December 28, triggering the December 31 GRNI accrual — entered without its auto-reverse flag. Meridian's invoice arrives and is entered in January, matching cleanly against a PO and receipt that were always correct, while the unreversed December accrual quietly remains.

questions.prompt: Select every statement that correctly matches one of Elena Marsh's January 31 symptoms to its actual root cause.
options: 'AP aging doesn't match the GL' traces to the unreversed December GRNI accrual journal.
'Harborview's invoice shows overdue despite a payment I saw' traces to the duplicated EFT bank transmission.
'Depreciation looks heavier than expected' traces to FA-10452 being capitalized under the wrong asset category.
'A $9,200.00 bank item is still open' traces to a network timeout retry on the bank's own ACH processor.
'Intercompany numbers between the US and Canada don't tie' traces to the missing Subledger Accounting Account Rule for account 7850.
questions.explain: The AP mismatch traces to the unreversed GRNI journal, the heavy depreciation traces to FA-10452's miscategorization, and the bank item traces to the ACH processor's duplicate transmission. Harborview's invoice-looks-unpaid symptom actually traces to the misapplied cash receipt, not the bank duplicate. The intercompany mismatch traces to the unposted INTERCO-JAN-0131 journal, not the missing Account Rule — that rule gap is what caused the separate 'Receivables transactions missing from GL' symptom.

questions.prompt: Investigating the AP aging mismatch, you check account 2150 (Accrued Liabilities) for Company 1000, cost center 420, and find two entries tied to the same purchase order. What does this confirm, and by how much is the GL's Accrued Liabilities balance overstated?
options: JE-GRNI-1231's December accrual never reversed, and the GL's Accrued Liabilities balance is overstated by $18,400.00 — the same amount as the Meridian bearings liability counted twice.
Two separate suppliers both billed LTV for the same bearings order, and the GL is overstated by $36,800.00.
The December receipt was recorded twice by Priya Nandan, and the GL's Accrued Liabilities balance is overstated by $9,200.00.
JE-GRNI-1231 posted with the wrong Company segment value, and the GL's Accrued Liabilities balance is overstated by $27,750.00.
questions.explain: The two entries tied to the same PO are JE-GRNI-1231 ($18,400.00, December) and the accounting generated by INV-MER-88341's validation ($18,400.00, January) — the same bearings liability counted twice because the accrual never reversed. The AP subledger's own aging only reflects the validated invoice, so the GL's Accrued Liabilities balance is $18,400.00 higher than it should be.

questions.prompt: Checking Harborview's AR aging detail invoice by invoice, instead of by total balance, and the receipt application history for RCPT-50231 confirms the root cause of the AR confusion. What does this evidence actually show?
options: RCPT-50231's full $55,100.00 was applied to INV-HV-29890 instead of INV-HV-30144, even though the total cash and total AR balance for Harborview were never wrong.
RCPT-50231 was never recorded at all, so neither invoice shows any payment applied.
RCPT-50231 was split evenly between both invoices, leaving each one partially paid.
Harborview's total AR balance is understated by $49,000.00 because of the misapplication.
questions.explain: The receipt application history confirms RCPT-50231 was applied in full to INV-HV-29890 by mistake, not INV-HV-30144. The total cash and total AR control balance were never affected — only the invoice-level detail was wrong, which is exactly why checking aging by total balance alone would have missed it.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: after FA-10452 is investigated and later reclassified, January's correct depreciation amount is $________, not the $2,416.67 it was originally miscalculated at.
questions.explain: Under the correct Manufacturing Equipment — Machinery category, a 10-year (120-month) useful life, $145,000.00 divided by 120 months gives a correct monthly depreciation of $1,208.33.

questions.prompt: Match each confirmed root cause to the fix lesson 21 actually applies to correct it.
left: JE-GRNI-1231's auto-reverse flag was never set
RCPT-50231 was applied to the wrong invoice
FA-10452 was capitalized to the wrong category and cost center
No Account Rule mapped account 7850 for Freight Charge transactions
INTERCO-JAN-0131 was left in Draft status
right: Sarah Lindqvist adds the missing mapping line and reruns Create Accounting
A manual reversing journal, JE-REV-0131, is entered for $18,400.00
Victor Okafor reviews and submits the journal for posting
Mateo Rios unapplies and reapplies the receipt to the correct invoice
Derek Shaw processes a reclassification transaction, effective the original placed-in-service date
questions.explain: The stale GRNI accrual is fixed with reversing journal JE-REV-0131. The misapplied receipt is unapplied and reapplied by Mateo Rios. The miscategorized asset is corrected with a reclassification transaction from Derek Shaw. The missing Account Rule mapping is added by Sarah Lindqvist, who then reruns Create Accounting. The unposted intercompany journal is reviewed and submitted by Victor Okafor.

questions.prompt: Of the six root causes confirmed in lessons 19-20, which one is resolved without making any correcting entry inside Oracle Fusion at all?
options: The $9,200.00 bank item — Regions Bank confirms the duplicate transmission in writing and reverses the debit itself.
The unreversed GRNI accrual — JE-REV-0131 is entered to reverse it.
The misapplied cash receipt — Mateo Rios unapplies and reapplies it.
The unposted intercompany journal — Victor Okafor submits it for posting.
questions.explain: The $9,200.00 bank variance is a bank-side processing error, not an LTV posting error. Its fix requires Regions Bank's own written confirmation and reversal of the duplicate debit — the only one of the six fixes that involves no correcting transaction inside Oracle Fusion.

questions.prompt: Lesson 20 notes that its three root causes are deliberately different in kind. Select every statement that correctly pairs a root cause with its kind.
options: The $9,200.00 bank variance is a processing error that happened entirely outside Oracle Fusion, on the bank's own systems.
The missing Account Rule for account 7850 is a configuration gap inside Subledger Accounting.
The unposted intercompany journal is also a configuration gap, the same kind of problem as the missing Account Rule.
The unposted intercompany journal is a simple human step — submitting a completed journal for posting — that never happened.
The $9,200.00 bank variance is caused by LTV posting the same payment twice inside Oracle Fusion.
questions.explain: The bank variance is a processing error outside Oracle Fusion entirely. The missing Account Rule is a genuine configuration gap inside Subledger Accounting. The intercompany journal, by contrast, was complete and balanced and simply never submitted — a human step that never happened, not a configuration problem. LTV's own payment records were never duplicated; the duplication happened at the bank.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of completing LTV's first month-end close, per lesson 21, in the order the lesson applies them.
items: Enter JE-REV-0131 to reverse the stale December GRNI accrual
Unapply RCPT-50231 from INV-HV-29890 and reapply it to INV-HV-30144
Reclassify FA-10452 from Office Equipment/cost center 410 to Manufacturing Equipment/cost center 420
Record Regions Bank's written confirmation and reversal of the duplicate $9,200.00 debit
Add the missing Account Rule mapping for account 7850 and rerun Create Accounting
Rerun the trial balance for both ledgers and close period Jan-26
questions.explain: Lesson 21 applies the six fixes in this order — AP, then AR, then Assets, then Cash Management, then Subledger Accounting, then the intercompany journal — and only after every item is resolved and verified does Victor Okafor rerun the trial balance for both ledgers and close period Jan-26.

questions.prompt: In lesson 23's final presentation, Elena Marsh hears the headline before any mechanics. Which of these correctly reflects the headline lesson 23 actually uses?
options: All six issues are identified, corrected, and verified, and period Jan-26 is closed and reconciled in both ledgers.
Six unrelated system failures occurred, and three of them are still being investigated.
The books balance now because Oracle Fusion automatically corrected the errors overnight.
Four of the six issues are fixed, and two will carry over into February's close.
questions.explain: Lesson 23's structure leads with exactly this headline — all six issues identified, corrected, and verified, with Jan-26 closed and reconciled in both ledgers — before getting into any mechanics, because Elena needs the bottom line first, not a lesson in Oracle Fusion internals.

questions.prompt: Lesson 24 notes that LTV's Oracle Fusion instance processed every Chapter 2 transaction without a single system error, yet Requirement 5 still failed on the first attempt. What does this gap actually illustrate?
options: A system that runs without errors isn't automatically a system that meets its requirements — Requirement 5 needed every subledger to actually reconcile to the GL, not just for transactions to post.
Oracle Fusion's error-checking is unreliable, since it should have caught all six problems automatically.
Requirement 5 was poorly written by Elena Marsh and should have been removed from the requirements list.
The six problems prove that Chapter 1's configuration was fundamentally broken from the start.
questions.explain: Every Chapter 2 transaction posted cleanly with no system errors, and Requirement 5 still failed on the first attempt — because a clean close requires every subledger to actually reconcile to the GL, which is a higher bar than 'nothing crashed.' Reviewing finished work against the actual requirement, not against whether anything errored out, is what catches that gap.

questions.prompt: Match each of Elena Marsh's five original requirements (lesson 2) to what lesson 24 confirms was built to satisfy it.
left: A chart of accounts supporting intercompany elimination
Supplier, customer, bank, and asset master data
A full month of real transactions
right: Met, but only after an investigation and correction cycle in lessons 18-21, not on the first attempt
Two legal entities, two primary ledgers, two business units — one full stack per entity
Purchasing through payment, invoicing through cash receipt, asset capitalization through depreciation, bank reconciliation, and GL posting
The five-segment design with Company as the balancing segment and Intercompany mirroring it
Four suppliers, three customers, two bank accounts, five asset categories, two asset books
questions.explain: Requirement 1 (two-entity structure) maps to the two legal entities, ledgers, and business units from lessons 3-4. Requirement 2 (chart of accounts) maps to the five-segment design from lesson 5. Requirement 3 (master data) maps to the suppliers, customers, bank accounts, and asset categories from lessons 6-8. Requirement 4 (a full month of transactions) maps to lessons 9-17's purchasing-through-posting cycle. Requirement 5 (a clean close) was only met after lessons 18-21's investigation and correction cycle, not on the first attempt.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: lesson 25 says this capstone closes the Capstone stage, and the Oracle Fusion Financials Consultant path's final stage is ________.
acceptedAnswers: Oracle Financials Career and Interview Preparation
questions.explain: Lesson 25 names the path's final stage as Oracle Financials Career & Interview Preparation — covering terminology, functional and scenario-based interview questions, troubleshooting and implementation questions, resume project descriptions, and certification prep.

questions.prompt: Lesson 25 argues that a new consultant's instinct to hide the six-problem month-end crisis from an interviewer is the wrong instinct. Why, specifically, does the lesson say the crisis should be presented as a strength?
options: Because it's the part of the capstone that proves you can diagnose and fix a system when it isn't working, not just configure one correctly the first time.
Because interviewers are more interested in system failures than in successful configurations.
Because the crisis makes the capstone sound more difficult than the other courses in the path.
Because hiding the crisis would be dishonest, even though it doesn't actually demonstrate any useful skill.
questions.explain: Lesson 25 is explicit that the six-problem crisis is the single most interview-relevant part of the whole capstone, because it proves the skill real consultants are actually hired for: not just configuring a system correctly the first time, but diagnosing and fixing one when it isn't — exactly what every earlier module course only tested in isolation.
